newsitem.title: GERMANY: OECD chief urges Germany to push through cuts.
newsitem.headline: OECD chief urges Germany to push through cuts.

text.p: The new head of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on Tuesday urged Germany to push through government savings while maintaining the social fairness of austerity measures.

Donald Johnston, visiting Bonn for the first time as the OECD secretary general, praised the passage of key parts of a 70 billion mark deficit-cutting package last week by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition government.
"The OECD would applaud the achievement of bringing that programme to fruition," Johnston said after meeting government officials in Bonn.
Echoing the conclusions of a recent OECD Germany country survey, Johnston said more savings were needed.
"When we talk about further cuts...there's a general recognition that fiscal consolidation is desirable," Johnston said, adding that slimming down governments was a key OECD goal.

Germany, in a bid to meet the Maastricht treaty's terms on qualifying for European monetary union, plans to cut its budget deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product next year from an expected four percent this year.
Maastricht says that deficits should be close to or below three percent of GDP in 1997 if a country is to participate in the 1999 launch of the single European currency.
Johnston said "social equity" must be maintained alongside efforts to promote growth in implementing austerity measures.

He said he did not see any risk of a social backlash among OECD member states in Europe striving to join EMU, saying that governments were showing "sensitivity" in their efforts to reduce deficits in order to qualify.
Johnston was visiting Germany on a two-day familiarisation trip and said the OECD had not yet made any revisions to its half-yearly country report released in early September.
The report said Germany could qualify for EMU as long as it fully implemented Kohl's spending cuts.
It predicted German economic growth of 0.5 percent this year and 2.4 percent next year -- but said those figures were likely to be revised upwards in October following a strong second quarter.
Johnston said he supported a call by Bonn for an increase in German staffing at the OECD secretariat in Paris to reflect Germany's financial contributions.
Germans now make up seven percent of the secretariat staff, against membership fees of 11 percent, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a statement.
